project.title: What if the sky disappeared?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science and space shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If the air stayed but stopped scattering sunlight, what would a day on your street be like?
project.viewer_takeaway: The blue sky is sunlight scattered by air; it lights every shadow and makes dusk and dawn gradual. Without it, shade turns dangerously dark and days switch on and off.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: Air molecules scatter sunlight, blue most strongly (Rayleigh scattering), and haze adds whiter scattering. That scattered light is the blue sky; it lights shade on a clear day and keeps lighting the sky after sunset as twilight.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: At noon on a clear equinox day at about 30°N, air and haze stop scattering visible sunlight. Air composition, pressure, breathing, refraction, weather and clouds are otherwise unchanged; the film stages a cloudless day.
assumptions: Scattering stops instantly and everywhere; absorption by ozone and water vapour continues.
Clouds would still scatter, but the staged day is cloudless.
Street geometry: east-west canyon, 14 m road, 16-26 m buildings, sun 60 degrees high at noon.
The near miss and the people are illustrative authored events, not predictions.
causal_chain: Sunlight no longer scatters off air, so the daytime sky is black and the sun appears as a white disc among stars.
Shade loses its main light source, skylight, and is lit only by light reflected from sunlit surfaces.
Sun-adapted eyes see that shade as near-black, like a tunnel entrance, and drivers may not see people standing in it.
Eyes that adapt in deep shade can see bright stars at noon.
Without scattering the setting sun does not redden and there is no twilight, so ground light falls from sunlight to starlight as the disc sets, and returns at sunrise without dawn.
uncertainties: Shade light depends strongly on street geometry and surface reflectance; the 20 percent and 45 times figures are estimates for this street.
How many stars a person would see depends on glare, adaptation and the sun direction.
Ozone and water-vapour absorption would tint and dim the setting sun slightly.
Longer-term climate and ecological effects are outside this film.

claims.statement: The blue daytime sky is sunlight scattered by air molecules, which scatter shorter wavelengths more strongly.
claims.reasoning: Rayleigh scattering by molecules much smaller than the wavelength scales roughly with the inverse fourth power of wavelength.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Say the blue is sunlight bouncing off air; do not claim the sky is a physical layer.

claims.statement: On a clear day, skylight is the main source of light in open shade; light reflected from sunlit surfaces adds the rest.
claims.reasoning: Shaded surfaces receive no direct beam; diffuse sky radiation is defined as the scattered solar radiation reaching the ground from the whole sky.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Shadows lose most of their light, not all of it.

claims.statement: With scattering switched off, the daytime sky would look black, as it does from the Moon, while direct sunlight stays as strong or slightly stronger and whiter.
claims.reasoning: With no scattered light, only the solar disc and stars are visible; scattering no longer removes blue from the direct beam.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Keep breathing, pressure and weather unchanged; this is a fictional optical change only.

claims.statement: In this street canyon the shade would fall to roughly one fifth of its normal light, making sunlit pavement about 45 times brighter than shade instead of about 10 times.
claims.reasoning: View-factor estimate for a 22 m wide canyon with 20 m buildings: about 6.7 klx of skylight plus 1.9 klx reflected light in shade becomes about 1.9 klx, against about 87 klx on sunlit horizontal pavement.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Present the numbers as this street’s telemetry, not a universal constant; shade is very dark, not perfectly black.

claims.statement: Drivers adapted to daylight can be unable to see into a much darker tunnel entrance, the black hole effect, which is why tunnel entrances are lit more brightly.
claims.reasoning: Road tunnel lighting practice reinforces entrance lighting because eyes cannot adapt instantly to large luminance drops.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Use as an analogy for crossing into deep shade.

claims.statement: A pedestrian standing in such shade could be very hard for a sun-adapted driver to see until they step into sunlight.
claims.reasoning: Shade luminance about 2-4 percent of the sunlit road is below typical tunnel threshold-zone ratios, where contrast detection fails.
claims.presentation_guardrail: The near miss is one illustrative event; say "even from drivers", not that every driver will hit someone.

claims.statement: Bright stars and planets could be seen in the black daytime sky from deep shade once the eyes adapt, but not from the sunlit glare.
claims.reasoning: With a black sky, glare and adaptation limit star visibility; Apollo crews rarely saw stars on the sunlit lunar surface but reported bright stars from shadow.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Show bright stars from shade, not a full Milky Way in sunlight.

claims.statement: Sunset colours come from scattering along the long low-sun path; without scattering the setting sun would stay nearly white and there would be no coloured glow.
claims.reasoning: Reddening of the low sun is caused by scattering removing blue light along the path; ozone and water vapour absorption would remain but are weaker in the visible.

claims.statement: Twilight is sunlight scattered by the upper atmosphere after sunset; without it, ground light would fall from sunlight to starlight in the roughly 2.5 minutes the disc takes to set at 30°N, instead of fading over about 25 minutes of civil twilight.
claims.reasoning: The sun sinks about 13 degrees per hour at 30°N on an equinox: 0.53 degrees takes about 2.5 minutes and 6 degrees about 28 minutes.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Night "drops" refers to the end of direct sunlight; moonlight and airglow are not shown.

claims.statement: Sunrise would likewise go from starlight to direct sunlight as soon as the disc clears the horizon, with no dawn glow beforehand.
claims.reasoning: The same geometry applies in reverse; only the direct beam lights the ground.
claims.presentation_guardrail: The sky stays black after sunrise.

creative_direction.logline: The sky goes black at noon but the air stays: shade turns into blind spots, sunsets lose their colour, and days start switching on and off.
creative_direction.visual_identity: One coastal street seen like an Apollo photograph with Earth’s air: blazing stone, black shadows, a white sun among stars, then a colourless sunset over the sea and a sunrise like a switch.
creative_direction.lighting: Physically separated sun key, skylight fill, ground bounce and haze; removing skylight empties shadows. Eye-adaptation exposure ramps in shade; ACES finish, bloom only on the sun and lamps.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level 1.45-1.65 m handheld POVs, a low shadow-edge dolly, a driver POV and locked telephotos; a move reveals, follows or compares, otherwise holds.
creative_direction.motion_language: Distance-driven walking, natural reactions (stop, look up, breathe, shade eyes), analytic car braking, compressed sun motion, staggered light switching.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: One metre-scale street throughout; true sun angular size and 30°N equinox altitudes with compressed clock time at sunset and sunrise.
creative_direction.opening_hook: You step outside at noon, and the sky goes black.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Shade stops being a refuge: a driver adapted to the sunlit road cannot see you in it until you step into the light.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: Without scattering there is no dusk or dawn: night drops when the sun sets, and in the morning the sun switches on.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The final frame is a sunlit street under a black sky with a switch-clack; the opening replays the switch-off as the blue drains.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the classic city street, Humanoid rig, sky dome, starfield and ocean; build one reusable sun/skylight lighting rig; story props (driver dash, promenade) from modeling helpers.

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original sparse score: airy midday pad that collapses with the sky, low heartbeat tension in the shade, a glassy star shimmer, cold open fifths at sunset, and a bright switch-on chord at sunrise.
audio.sfx_direction: City bed ducks 0.3 s before the sky drains, the near miss and the night drop; brake thump and horn on the near miss; deep sub drop at sunset; staggered window and lamp switch clicks 120-140 ms apart; switch clack at sunrise.

Sun 60 degrees high in the south (-X, slightly west), white, direct beam unchanged; sky-dome-v1 scatter 1 -> 0 at the event, starfield-v1 above, no aerial haze afterwards.

camera.movement: Slow tilt up the sunlit north facades into the black sky strip.
camera.lens_notes: Sunlit rooftops glow at the bottom; stars multiply as the eyes adapt.

subjects.appearance: Bright stars and planets in the black daytime sky; fainter ones appear as eyes adapt.
subjects.geometry_and_material: Seeded additive point sprites, brightness tied to the eye-adaptation exposure.
subjects.scale_and_accuracy: Only the brightest stars are shown in sunlit views, consistent with glare limits.
subjects.movement: Brightness 0.4 -> 2.6 as adaptation proceeds; planet-bright points first.

distribution.primary_search_intent: what if the sky disappeared, why is the sky blue, no atmosphere scattering, stars during the day
distribution.distinctive_angle: The air stays and only its glow disappears: the consequences are optical and personal, from blind spots in shade to sunsets that end like a switch.
distribution.comment_bait_question: Which would you miss first: blue sky, sunsets, or being able to see in the shade?
distribution.seo_integrity_note: Fictional optical premise with breathing, pressure and weather unchanged; shade and visibility figures are estimates for one street; the near miss is an illustrative event.
